To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have characterized a transmission event of HSV1 from father to son and found that these strains have nearly identical genome sequences and phenotypes, despite being isolated 17 years apart and in a different host.

we have characterized the full genome sequences of two strains of HSV-1 that were likely transmitted from father to son 17 years prior to their isolation, and that these viruses have preserved nearly identical sequences and phenotypes in the new hosts for decades.
the HSV-1 genomes of a father and son that were likely transmitted to each other 17 years ago have preserved their genotype and phenotype nearly perfectly.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic diversity of herpesviruses in humans.
the transmission, evolution and adaptation of human pathogens, and the impact of this on human disease.
understanding the mechanisms by which HSV-1 adapts to the host environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HSV genome is highly conserved over decades in the same host and over a single transmission event, and this conservation is associated with the retention of the in vivo phenotype.
these two strains of HSV-1 are identical in sequence and phenotype.
the HSV-1 strains from this father and son are identical.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the HSV-1 genome is remarkably resistant to change over the long term in a single host.
HSV-1 is a highly stable and conservative virus in terms of genome identity and phenotype.

we have shown that HSV-1 can be transmitted from a father to his son, that the virus can be maintained in both hosts, that the viral genome is conserved over decades of recurrences in the same individual, and that the phenotype is conserved as well, as demonstrated by the ability of these viruses to replicate in a mouse occlusion model.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the HSV-1 genome is remarkably stable during the course of a chronic infection in one human host, and that transmission of HSV-1 to a new host results in nearly perfect conservation of viral genotype and phenotype.

HSV-1 is remarkably conserved over time, even during episodes of transmission, and that it remains to be determined whether this is due to host immune selection, or to a lack of genetic diversity in HSV-1.

, in this instance, HSV-1 is a highly conservative virus in its ability to adapt to new hosts, and in its ability to preserve its phenotype and genotype during transmission and over decades of chronic disease.
